title: How to Evaluate Vendor EHR Integrations: A Guide for RCM Leaders
summary: An RCM software vendor's EHR integration is a core capability. Evaluate these 11 factors, including HL7/FHIR compatibility, security, and workflow fit.
body_markdown:
Choosing new revenue cycle management (RCM) or patient billing software means evaluating the ability to deliver on its functional promise, fit existing workflows, meet regulatory requirements, and connect cleanly to the electronic health record (EHR) at the center of the operation. A platform that solves a real problem on paper can still fail in practice if its EHR integration is shallow or clunky.
‍


This matters because the EHR is a nearly universal infrastructure. As of 2021, almost all non-federal acute care hospitals and more than three-quarters of office-based physicians had adopted a certified EHR. The EHR sits at the center of clinical and financial workflows, and the value of any new technology depends on how reliably it reads from and writes to that system.
‍


For revenue cycle leaders, the stakes are concrete: poor integration leads to duplicate data entry, billing errors, and revenue leakage. Strong integration accelerates cash flow, reduces administrative burden, and protects the patient experience.
‍


Use this guide to evaluate a vendor's EHR integration, including 11 specific factors to evaluate and the steps in the buying process that surface meaningful differences among vendors.


‍


## What Is an EHR Integration?


An **Electronic Health Record (EHR)** is a digital version of a patient's medical history that consolidates data from multiple providers into a single record, providing access to patient histories, test results, medications, and treatment plans across care settings.
‍


An **Electronic Medical Record (EMR)** is similar but limited to a single practice. **Practice Management (PM)** systems handle the administrative and financial side of care, i.e. scheduling, billing, claims, and collection of demographic information. In many practices, these systems are bundled together.
‍


**EHR integration is the process of connecting an EHR with other healthcare systems so information can flow across platforms in real-time.** For revenue cycle leaders, the most important EHR integrations move balances, payments, adjustments, and demographic information bidirectionally[between the EHR/PM and the billing platform](https://collectly.co/blog/5-gaps-in-ehr-only-patient-billing-rcm) .
‍


Effective integration keeps records synchronized, eliminates manual data entry, and enables specialized tools to operate from a single source of truth. Common examples of fragmentation include laboratory and radiology information systems, pharmacy systems for e-prescribing, and patient-facing tools for scheduling,[eligibility verification, intake](https://www.collectly.co/blog/patient-intake-rcm-strategies) , and billing.
‍


Without effective integrations between EHRs and billing systems, staff end up reconciling data manually—at the cost of time and effort that could be spent on more valuable admin work.[The 2025 CAQH Index estimates the industry can still save $21 billion a year by automating remaining manual administrative transactions.](https://www.hfma.org/technology/4-steps-healthcare-cfos-can-take-to-improve-interoperability/)


Many[EHR/EMR/PM systems include basic RCM functions](https://collectly.co/blog/5-gaps-in-ehr-only-patient-billing-rcm) , like tracking charges out and payments in—but EHR systems are built to store clinical data, document care, and maintain compliance. EHRs are not built to be consumer-grade payment systems, deliver personalized patient financial experiences, or provide detailed[RCM KPI analyses](https://www.collectly.co/blog/rcm-kpis-healthcare-finance) . This is where an RCM software vendor, plus a strong EHR integration, can fill the gap.


‍


## 11 Key Factors to Evaluate in a Vendor's EHR Integration


‍


Vendors describe their integrations in roughly the same way: "works with leading EHRs," "bidirectional sync," "HIPAA-compliant." Look closer at these 11 factors to understand the real differences among EHR integrations:


‍


### 1. The Integration Actually Exists


Vendors often market an integration that exists for one or two major EHRs but rely on flat-file uploads, manual exports, or outsourced labor for everything else. Ask the vendor to demonstrate the integration in your EHR's environment. Confirm which fields are read, which are written, how often the sync runs, and what triggers it. If the answer involves a nightly batch or a CSV, that is not real-time integration.


‍


### 2. Integration With Your Specific EHR


Verify that the vendor has a production integration with the exact EHR and version your organization runs, and that it supports your specialty. A vendor with a strong Epic integration may have only basic capabilities in athenahealth or NextGen, and a billing integration built for primary care may not handle the encounter structure of radiology or behavioral health. Request a reference customer on the same EHR and a similar specialty, and ask about edge cases.


‍


### 3. Functionality, Ease of Use, and Workflow Fit


Strong integration should reduce administrative work, not add to it. Staff should not need to double-document or fill in fields manually because the integration only covers part of the record.


Look for bidirectional integrations, through which data flows both ways in real time. This eliminates manual double-entry and reconciliation errors, keeping both systems as a single source of truth so staff aren't chasing discrepancies between what the clinical record shows and what billing actually collected.


Watch a demo of scenarios that[fit your team’s common workflows](https://www.collectly.co/blog/revenue-cycle-management-rcm-workflows-for-healthcare-providers) , and note every place[a human has to bridge a gap](https://www.collectly.co/blog/ai-in-revenue-cycle-the-real-test-is-workflow-completion) . Those are the spots that erode adoption over time.


‍


### 4. Regulatory Compliance


Any integration must comply with HIPAA, HITECH,[CMS interoperability rules](https://www.cms.gov/newsroom/fact-sheets/interoperability-and-patient-access-fact-sheet) , and any state or regional data privacy laws that apply (such as CCPA for California or GDPR for European operations). Confirm that the vendor's data handling, business associate agreement (BAA), and breach notification processes meet your organization's standards.


‍


### 5. Data Security


Verify the integration uses encryption for data at rest and in transit, role-based access controls, and audit logging. Ask about third-party certifications: HITRUST (i1 or r2), SOC 2 Type II, and ISO 27001 are the strongest signals that a vendor has been independently reviewed.[Healthcare data breaches](https://www.hipaajournal.com/healthcare-data-breach-statistics/) are a significant ongoing issue, and security should be a key discussion point from the very start.


‍


### 6. Data Storage Model


Understand where EHR data resides once it moves through the integration (on-premises, cloud, or vendor-hosted), each with different cost, security, and IT support needs. Confirm where data is stored, who has access, and how it is segregated from other customers' data. Surface IT constraints—including data residency, specific cloud providers, and FedRAMP—early.


‍


### 7. Industry-Standard Data Exchange


Modern integrations often use established healthcare standards for applicable services:[HL7](https://www.hl7.org/implement/standards/index.cfm?ref=nav) for messaging,[FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources)](https://www.hl7.org/fhir/) for API-based exchange, and[DICOM](https://www.dicomstandard.org/current) for medical imaging. FHIR has become the dominant standard for new integrations and is required by recent CMS interoperability rules. Vendors should also provide technical documentation and developer support if your team plans to build on the integration.


‍


### 8. Customer Support and SLAs


Ask about support availability, channels, response and resolution SLAs, and escalation paths. Go beyond the SLA on paper to understand the real-world support experience. A 4-hour response SLA means nothing if the first response is always a request for more information.


‍


### 9. Implementation Support


Ask what implementation looks like: who manages it, how long it takes, what is required from your team, and what testing happens before go-live. Look for named implementation leads, structured timelines, and live-environment validation. A vendor that goes live in 4-8 weeks operates at a different level than one quoting 6 months and a dedicated internal project manager.


‍


### 10. Contingencies and Fallback Options


Even strong integrations occasionally fail. Sync errors, EHR upgrades, and edge cases happen. Ask whether the platform supports bulk uploads or manual corrections when real-time sync isn't an option, how the vendor handles EHR version upgrades, and what notice you'll get before a breaking change. The answer reveals[how mature the integration really is](https://www.collectly.co/blog/patient-billing-maturity-model) .


‍


### 11. Reviews and User Scores


Independent reviews can help verify vendor claims. Look for sources like KLAS, NPS data, Trustpilot, and platform-specific marketplaces to understand patterns in user experiences and reviews. Pay particular attention to reviews that mention the integration specifically (e.g., APIs, sync reliability, and support response on integration issues) to surface realities that don’t come up in a demo.


‍


## EHR Integration Evaluation: Step-by-Step Process


‍


The factors above describe what to evaluate. The process below describes how to evaluate. Follow these steps for strong decision-making:


1. **Document the need.** Document the problems the software has to solve, the workflows it must support, and the outcomes that define success. This becomes the evaluation rubric.
2. **If replacing, map the contract cycle.** Review the current contract's end date and notice requirements, identify the ideal cutover date, and work backward to set evaluation and implementation deadlines.
3. **Set SMART goals.** Define specific, measurable targets: reduction in days in A/R, increase in point-of-service collections, decrease in billing inquiries, staff hours recovered.
4. **Assess integration requirements.** Catalog the EHR, PM, and adjacent systems the new platform must connect to. Note version numbers, customizations, and any in-flight migrations.
5. **Evaluate the EHR integration.** Use the 11 factors above. Document each vendor's answers and request demonstrations of key functions.
6. **Review IT and security.** Engage IT and security teams early to confirm data standards (HL7, FHIR, DICOM), compliance, encryption, access controls, and certifications. Surface objections before contracting.
7. **Review operational impact.** Walk through what changes for front-desk staff, billers, and patient access teams, and how many manual steps are eliminated.
8. **Perform market research.** Look at industry analyst coverage (KLAS, Gartner, Forrester), independent reviews, and trade publications.
9. **Speak to reference customers.** Prioritize customers on the same EHR, in a similar specialty, at a similar scale. Ask about the integration and what hasn't gone well.
10. **Evaluate the total cost of ownership.** Look beyond the subscription fee: implementation, ongoing IT support, training, and staff time to maintain the integration.
11. **Conduct product demos.** Use real workflows and real data scenarios. Invite the staff who will actually use the platform.
12. **Compare vendors and select.** Score each vendor against the rubric, weight by what matters most to your organization, and make the call.


‍
